title: Designing a Secure Architecture on AWS
content: The security pillar of the AWS Well-Architected Framework recommends a strong identity foundation built on IAM roles and least-privilege policies. Encrypt data at rest with AWS KMS, enable CloudTrail for auditing every API call, isolate workloads in separate VPCs and accounts using AWS Organizations, and automate detection with GuardDuty. Security architecture on Amazon Web Services is layered: protect the network edge, the compute layer, and the data itself.

title: Serverless Computing with AWS Lambda
content: AWS Lambda runs code in response to events without provisioning servers. You pay per invocation and per millisecond of execution. Cold starts happen when a new execution environment must be initialised, adding latency to the first request; provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm. Serverless functions fit event-driven workloads such as image processing, webhooks and scheduled jobs.

title: Multi-Cloud Strategy and Vendor Lock-In
content: Organisations increasingly spread workloads across Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and AWS. A multi-cloud strategy reduces dependence on a single provider and can satisfy data residency rules in the European Union, but it adds operational complexity. Portable abstractions such as containers and Terraform modules help, while proprietary managed services increase lock-in.

title: Autoscaling and Elasticity
content: Elasticity means capacity follows demand. Auto Scaling groups add or remove virtual machines based on CPU utilisation, request count or custom metrics. Target tracking policies keep a metric near a set point, and predictive scaling uses historical traffic to launch instances before a known peak, such as Black Friday. Scaling in too aggressively can cause thrashing.

title: Cloud Cost Optimization with FinOps
content: FinOps brings finance and engineering together to control cloud spending. Typical savings come from rightsizing over-provisioned instances, buying reserved instances or savings plans for steady workloads, running fault-tolerant batch jobs on spot instances, and deleting idle resources. Tagging every resource makes it possible to attribute the monthly bill to teams.

title: Amazon S3 Storage Classes and Lifecycle Policies
content: Amazon S3 stores objects in buckets and is designed for eleven nines of durability. Storage classes trade retrieval speed for price: S3 Standard for hot data, S3 Standard-IA for infrequently accessed data and S3 Glacier for archives. Lifecycle policies automatically transition objects between classes or expire them after a number of days. Versioning protects against accidental overwrites.

title: The Shared Responsibility Model
content: In the shared responsibility model the cloud provider secures the physical data centres, hypervisors and global network, while the customer is responsible for what they put in the cloud: identity configuration, operating system patches, firewall rules and data classification. Most cloud breaches stem from customer misconfiguration such as publicly readable storage buckets.

title: Identity Federation with Microsoft Entra ID
content: Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure Active Directory, provides single sign-on for thousands of SaaS applications. Federation through SAML or OpenID Connect lets employees use one corporate identity across cloud apps, while conditional access policies require multi-factor authentication from unmanaged devices. Centralised identity simplifies onboarding and offboarding.

title: Cloud Migration Strategies: The Six Rs
content: Moving on-premises applications to the cloud usually follows one of six strategies: rehost (lift and shift), replatform, repurchase, refactor, retire or retain. Rehosting is fastest but captures few cloud benefits; refactoring into cloud-native services takes longer but improves scalability. A discovery phase inventories servers and dependencies before any workload moves.

title: Edge Computing and Content Delivery Networks
content: Content delivery networks such as Amazon CloudFront and Cloudflare cache static assets in points of presence close to users, cutting round-trip time. Edge computing goes further by running code at those locations, for example to personalise responses or validate tokens without contacting the origin server. Cache hit ratio and time-to-first-byte are the key metrics.

title: Log4Shell: The Apache Log4j Vulnerability
content: CVE-2021-44228, known as Log4Shell, was disclosed in December 2021 and affected the Apache Log4j logging library used by countless Java applications. An attacker could trigger remote code execution by getting a crafted JNDI lookup string written to a log. Mitigation required upgrading Log4j to version 2.17 or later and blocking outbound LDAP traffic.

title: Defending Login Pages Against Credential Stuffing
content: Credential stuffing replays username and password pairs leaked from other breaches, while brute-force attacks try many guesses against a single account. Defences include rate limiting failed login attempts per IP address and per account, temporary account lockout, CAPTCHA challenges after repeated failures, checking new passwords against known breached lists, and enforcing multi-factor authentication.

title: Zero Trust Architecture
content: Zero trust replaces the idea of a trusted internal network with the principle never trust, always verify. Every request is authenticated, authorised and encrypted regardless of where it originates. NIST Special Publication 800-207 describes the reference architecture, and Google's BeyondCorp project showed that employees can work without a traditional VPN when device posture and identity are checked continuously.

title: Phishing and Email Authentication
content: Phishing emails impersonate trusted senders to steal credentials or deliver malware. Security awareness training helps staff spot suspicious links, but technical controls matter as well: SPF lists servers allowed to send for a domain, DKIM signs messages cryptographically, and DMARC tells receivers to reject spoofed mail that fails those checks.

title: Responding to a Ransomware Incident
content: The WannaCry outbreak in May 2017 encrypted files on hundreds of thousands of machines, including systems in the UK National Health Service. A ransomware response plan should isolate infected hosts, preserve forensic evidence, restore from offline backups that attackers cannot reach, and involve legal counsel before any decision about paying. Regular restore drills prove the backups actually work.

title: Preventing SQL Injection
content: SQL injection remains on the OWASP Top 10 list. It occurs when user input is concatenated directly into a database query, letting an attacker change the statement. Parameterised queries and prepared statements keep data separate from code, object-relational mappers help by default, and least-privilege database accounts limit the damage of a successful attack.

title: Encryption at Rest and in Transit
content: Data in transit should be protected with TLS 1.3, which removes legacy cipher suites and shortens the handshake. Data at rest is commonly encrypted with AES-256, with keys held in a hardware security module or a managed key service. Key rotation limits the amount of data exposed if a key leaks, and envelope encryption makes rotation cheap.

title: Threat Detection with SIEM
content: A security information and event management platform such as Splunk collects logs from servers, firewalls and identity providers, then correlates events to detect attacks in progress. Detection rules are often mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework so analysts can see which adversary techniques are covered. Alert fatigue is a real risk when rules are noisy.

title: Penetration Testing and Bug Bounty Programs
content: Penetration testers are hired to attack systems within an agreed scope and report weaknesses before criminals find them. Bug bounty platforms like HackerOne extend this to a crowd of independent researchers who are paid per valid finding. Clear rules of engagement and a responsible disclosure policy protect both the company and the researcher.

title: Software Supply Chain Attacks
content: In the SolarWinds incident discovered in December 2020, attackers inserted a backdoor into Orion software updates that were then distributed to around 18,000 customers. Supply chain attacks target build systems and dependencies instead of the victim directly. Countermeasures include a software bill of materials (SBOM), signed artifacts with Sigstore, pinned dependencies and hardened CI runners.

title: Speeding Up PostgreSQL Queries with Indexes
content: When a PostgreSQL query is slow, start with EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see whether the planner performs a sequential scan. B-tree indexes serve equality and range filters, GIN indexes accelerate full-text search and JSONB containment, and partial indexes cover only the rows a query needs. Every index also slows down writes, so index the access patterns that matter.

title: ACID Transactions and Isolation Levels
content: ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Isolation levels define which anomalies concurrent transactions may observe: read committed prevents dirty reads, repeatable read prevents non-repeatable reads, and serializable also prevents phantom reads at the cost of more aborts and retries. Choosing a level is a trade-off between correctness and throughput.

title: Document Databases and MongoDB
content: MongoDB stores data as flexible JSON-like documents instead of rows in fixed tables, so a schema can evolve without migrations. Relational databases enforce structure and support joins across normalised tables, while document stores favour embedding related data together and scaling out through sharding. NoSQL is a better fit when records are heterogeneous and access patterns are known in advance.

title: The CAP Theorem Explained
content: Formulated by Eric Brewer in 2000, the CAP theorem states that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency, availability and partition tolerance. Because network partitions happen, designers choose between consistency and availability during a partition. Apache Cassandra leans towards availability, while systems such as Google Spanner prioritise strong consistency.

title: Database Replication and Failover
content: Primary-replica replication copies every write from the primary to one or more replicas, which can serve read traffic and take over if the primary fails. Asynchronous replication introduces replication lag, so a read immediately after a write may return stale data. Automated failover tools promote a replica, but split-brain scenarios must be prevented with fencing.

title: Caching with Redis
content: Redis is an in-memory key-value store often placed in front of a relational database. In the cache-aside pattern, the application checks Redis first and only queries the database on a miss, then stores the result with a time-to-live. Eviction policies such as allkeys-lru decide what to drop when memory is full. Caching reduces read latency but introduces invalidation problems.

title: Sharding a Database Horizontally
content: Sharding splits a large dataset across several database servers so that each node holds only a subset of rows. A good shard key spreads load evenly; a poor one creates hot spots where one shard receives most of the traffic. Cross-shard queries and transactions become expensive, which is why many teams postpone sharding until vertical scaling is exhausted.

title: Troubleshooting MySQL Deadlocks
content: The error message Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction means InnoDB detected two transactions waiting on each other and rolled one back. Run SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS to see the latest deadlock, then make transactions acquire locks in a consistent order, keep them short, and add indexes so updates lock fewer rows. Applications should retry the failed transaction.

title: Data Warehousing with Snowflake and BigQuery
content: Analytical workloads (OLAP) scan many rows but few columns, so cloud data warehouses like Snowflake and Google BigQuery use columnar storage and separate compute from storage. Transactional systems (OLTP) handle many small reads and writes instead. Data is typically loaded through ELT pipelines and modelled into fact and dimension tables for reporting.

title: Vector Databases for Similarity Search
content: Vector databases such as Pinecone and Milvus store high-dimensional embeddings and answer approximate nearest neighbour queries. Index structures like HNSW graphs and inverted file indexes trade a small amount of recall for large speedups over brute-force comparison. Libraries such as FAISS from Meta provide the same algorithms in-process without a separate server.

title: The Transformer Architecture
content: The 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need by Vaswani and colleagues at Google introduced the Transformer, which replaced recurrence with self-attention. Each token attends to every other token through query, key and value projections, and multi-head attention lets the model capture different relationships in parallel. Positional encodings inject word order. Transformers now underpin most large language models.

title: BERT and Bidirectional Pretraining
content: BERT, released by Google in 2018, pretrains a Transformer encoder with a masked language modelling objective: random tokens are hidden and the model predicts them from context on both sides. A next sentence prediction task was also used. After pretraining, BERT is fine-tuned for classification, question answering and named entity recognition with a small task-specific head.

title: Sentence Embeddings for Semantic Search
content: Sentence-BERT, introduced by Reimers and Gurevych in 2019, trains siamese Transformer networks so that sentences with similar meaning map to nearby vectors. Semantic search encodes documents once, encodes each query at request time, and ranks documents by cosine similarity. Unlike keyword matching, it can match a query to a document that uses different words with the same meaning.

title: Overfitting and Regularization
content: A model overfits when it memorises noise in the training set and generalises poorly to unseen examples, visible as a growing gap between training and validation loss. Remedies include collecting more data, L1 or L2 weight penalties, dropout, data augmentation and early stopping based on a held-out validation set. Cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate on small datasets.

title: Gradient Boosting and XGBoost
content: Gradient boosting builds an ensemble of shallow decision trees where each new tree corrects the residual errors of the previous ones. XGBoost, created by Tianqi Chen, added regularisation, sparsity-aware split finding and efficient parallel training, and it dominated Kaggle competitions on tabular data. It also supports learning-to-rank objectives such as LambdaMART-style pairwise and NDCG ranking.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
content: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds a large language model in external knowledge. A retriever fetches relevant passages for the user question and the generator conditions its answer on them, which reduces hallucinations and allows citing sources. The quality of the final answer depends heavily on retrieval quality, chunking strategy and reranking of the passages.

title: Reinforcement Learning and AlphaGo
content: In reinforcement learning an agent learns a policy by taking actions in an environment and receiving rewards. DeepMind's AlphaGo combined deep neural networks with Monte Carlo tree search and defeated Lee Sedol at the game of Go in Seoul in March 2016. Its successor AlphaZero learned purely from self-play without human game records.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks for Computer Vision
content: Convolutional neural networks learn image features with small filters that slide across the input, sharing weights and capturing local patterns such as edges and textures. AlexNet won the ImageNet challenge in 2012 by a wide margin and started the deep learning boom in computer vision. Later architectures like ResNet used skip connections to train much deeper networks.

title: Evaluating Classification Models
content: Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced datasets, so classifiers are usually evaluated with precision, recall and the F1 score. Precision measures how many predicted positives are correct, recall measures how many actual positives were found. The ROC curve and its area under the curve summarise performance across decision thresholds, and a confusion matrix shows where errors occur.

title: Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning
content: Machine learning systems can reproduce historical bias present in their training data, for instance in hiring or lending decisions. Fairness audits compare error rates across demographic groups, and techniques such as reweighting and threshold adjustment can reduce disparities. The European Union AI Act classifies certain uses as high-risk and requires documentation and human oversight.

title: Microservices versus Monoliths
content: A monolith is deployed as a single unit, which keeps development and debugging simple early on. Microservices split the system into independently deployable services owned by small teams, enabling separate scaling and release cycles but introducing network calls, distributed tracing and data consistency challenges. Martin Fowler recommends starting with a monolith and extracting services when boundaries are clear.

title: Test-Driven Development
content: Test-driven development, popularised by Kent Beck, follows a short cycle: write a failing test, write just enough code to make it pass, then refactor. Writing the test first clarifies the intended behaviour and produces a safety net of unit tests that make later changes less risky. Critics note that TDD can slow exploratory work.

title: Effective Code Review
content: Code review catches defects and spreads knowledge across a team. Small pull requests on GitHub are reviewed faster and more thoroughly than large ones. Reviewers should focus on correctness, readability and design rather than style issues that a linter can enforce automatically, and comments should be specific and kind. Automated checks should pass before a human looks.

title: The SOLID Principles
content: Robert C. Martin collected five object-oriented design principles under the acronym SOLID: single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation and dependency inversion. Applied with judgement they produce code that is easier to extend and test, for example by depending on abstractions so that implementations can be swapped in unit tests.

title: Managing Technical Debt
content: Ward Cunningham coined the technical debt metaphor: shortcuts taken to ship faster accrue interest in the form of slower future changes. Not all debt is bad, but it should be visible and deliberate. Teams track it in the backlog, reserve capacity for refactoring each sprint, and pay it down when touching nearby code.

title: Designing REST APIs
content: A well-designed REST API models resources as nouns in URLs and uses HTTP methods for actions: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates and DELETE removes. Correct status codes such as 201, 404 and 409 make errors predictable. Versioning through the URL path or a header lets the API evolve without breaking clients, and idempotency keys make retries safe.

title: Classic Design Patterns
content: The 1994 book Design Patterns by the Gang of Four catalogued 23 reusable solutions to recurring object-oriented design problems. The factory pattern decouples object creation, the observer pattern notifies subscribers about state changes and the strategy pattern swaps algorithms at runtime. Overusing patterns can make simple code harder to follow.

title: Finding Memory Leaks in Java Applications
content: If a Java service's heap usage keeps climbing until it throws OutOfMemoryError, something is holding references that should be released. Capture a heap dump with jmap or the -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError flag and analyse it in Eclipse Memory Analyzer to find the dominating objects. Common culprits are unbounded caches, static collections and listeners that are never removed.

title: Semantic Versioning
content: Semantic versioning uses version numbers of the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increment the major version for incompatible API changes, the minor version for backwards-compatible features, and the patch version for bug fixes. Following the convention lets package managers resolve compatible dependency ranges automatically, and a changelog explains what changed.

title: Agile and Scrum
content: The Agile Manifesto, signed in 2001 in Snowbird, Utah, values individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change. Scrum organises work into fixed-length sprints with planning, daily stand-ups, a review and a retrospective. The product owner prioritises the backlog while the team decides how to deliver.

title: TCP versus UDP
content: TCP establishes a connection with a three-way handshake and guarantees ordered, reliable delivery through acknowledgements and retransmission, which suits web pages and file transfers. UDP sends independent datagrams without delivery guarantees, so it has lower overhead and latency, which suits voice calls, online gaming and live video where a late packet is useless anyway.

title: How DNS Resolution Works
content:
When you type a domain name, a recursive resolver queries the root servers, then the top-level domain servers, then the authoritative name server to find the A or AAAA record.

Answers are cached for their TTL. A NXDOMAIN response means the name does not exist, while SERVFAIL often points to a DNSSEC or upstream problem; dig and nslookup help troubleshoot. More at https://example.com/dns-guide

title: BGP and the 2021 Facebook Outage
content: The Border Gateway Protocol exchanges routing information between autonomous systems on the internet. On 4 October 2021 a faulty configuration change caused Facebook's backbone routers to withdraw the BGP routes to its DNS servers, taking Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp offline for about six hours. The incident showed how a single routing change can cascade globally.

title: Layer 4 and Layer 7 Load Balancing
content: A layer 4 load balancer forwards TCP or UDP connections based on IP address and port, which is fast and protocol-agnostic. A layer 7 load balancer such as NGINX or HAProxy understands HTTP, so it can route by path or header, terminate TLS and insert cookies for session affinity. Health checks remove failing backends from rotation automatically.

title: VPNs, IPsec and WireGuard
content: A virtual private network creates an encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network. Site-to-site IPsec tunnels connect branch offices to a data centre, while remote-access VPNs serve individual laptops. WireGuard is a newer protocol with a small codebase and modern cryptography that is faster to set up and audit than traditional IPsec configurations.

title: Subnetting and CIDR Notation
content: CIDR notation such as 10.0.0.0/16 describes an IPv4 network by its prefix length. A /24 block contains 256 addresses, of which a few are reserved. When designing a cloud VPC, plan non-overlapping address ranges for public and private subnets in each availability zone and leave room for growth and for peering with other networks.

title: The Move to IPv6
content: The free pool of IPv4 addresses held by IANA was exhausted in February 2011. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, giving an essentially unlimited address space, and removes the need for network address translation in many designs. Adoption has been gradual; dual-stack deployments run IPv4 and IPv6 side by side during the transition.

title: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC
content: HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over a single TCP connection, but a lost packet still stalls every stream, a problem called head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, a transport developed at Google on top of UDP that handles streams independently and combines the transport and TLS handshakes to reduce connection setup latency.

title: Troubleshooting Network Latency and Packet Loss
content: When an application feels slow, measure before guessing. Ping shows round-trip time and packet loss, traceroute and mtr reveal which hop introduces delay, and jitter matters for real-time traffic. Packet captures with Wireshark expose retransmissions caused by congestion or a faulty link. Compare results from several locations to separate local Wi-Fi issues from upstream problems.

title: Firewalls and Network Segmentation
content: Stateful firewalls track connections and only allow return traffic for sessions that were initiated from an allowed side. Segmenting a network into zones with VLANs or cloud security groups limits how far an attacker can move laterally after compromising one host. Default-deny rules with explicit allow lists are easier to audit than sprawling exceptions.

title: Building CI/CD Pipelines
content: Continuous integration runs the build and automated tests on every commit so integration problems surface within minutes. Continuous delivery extends the pipeline to package and deploy releases automatically to staging and production. Tools such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and Jenkins define pipelines as code, and fast feedback keeps developers merging small changes frequently.

title: Docker Containers Explained
content: Docker packages an application with its dependencies into an image built from a Dockerfile. Images consist of read-only layers that are cached and shared, so rebuilding after a small code change is fast. Containers share the host kernel, which makes them far lighter than virtual machines that each run a full guest operating system.

title: Kubernetes Orchestration Basics
content: Kubernetes, open-sourced by Google in 2014 and now maintained by the CNCF, schedules containers across a cluster. Pods are the smallest deployable unit, Deployments manage replica sets and rolling updates, and Services give pods a stable network identity. Its design draws on lessons from Borg, Google's internal cluster manager.

title: Fixing CrashLoopBackOff in Kubernetes
content: A pod in CrashLoopBackOff starts, exits, and is restarted by the kubelet with an increasing back-off delay. Run kubectl logs --previous to read the output of the crashed container and kubectl describe pod to check events. Typical causes are a missing environment variable or config file, a failing liveness probe, or the container being OOMKilled because its memory limit is too low.

title: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform
content: Terraform by HashiCorp describes infrastructure declaratively in HCL files. terraform plan shows the changes needed to reach the desired state and terraform apply executes them. The state file maps configuration to real resources; storing it remotely with locking prevents two engineers from applying conflicting changes at the same time. Modules package reusable components.

title: Monitoring and Observability with Prometheus
content: Prometheus scrapes time-series metrics from instrumented services and evaluates alerting rules, while Grafana visualises them on dashboards. Observability combines metrics, structured logs and distributed traces so engineers can ask new questions about system behaviour. Alerts should fire on user-facing symptoms such as error rate and latency rather than on every internal fluctuation.

title: Blue-Green and Canary Deployments
content: Blue-green deployment keeps two identical production environments and switches traffic from the old version to the new one in a single step, allowing instant rollback. A canary release instead routes a small percentage of users to the new version first and widens the rollout only if error rates and latency stay healthy. Feature flags complement both techniques.

title: GitOps with Argo CD
content: GitOps treats a Git repository as the single source of truth for the desired state of a cluster. Controllers such as Argo CD and Flux continuously compare the live Kubernetes state with the manifests in Git and reconcile any drift. Every change is a reviewed commit, which provides an audit trail and makes rollback as simple as reverting.

title: Site Reliability Engineering and Error Budgets
content: Site reliability engineering, described in Google's 2016 SRE book, applies software engineering to operations. Teams define service level objectives, and the error budget is the amount of unreliability the SLO allows. When the budget is spent, feature releases pause in favour of reliability work. SRE also aims to reduce toil, the repetitive manual work that scales with traffic.

title: Managing Secrets Safely
content: API keys, database passwords and certificates should never be committed to source control, where they persist in history. A secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager issues credentials at runtime, audits access and supports automatic rotation. Secret scanning in CI catches accidental leaks before they are pushed to a shared repository.

title: Amazon S3 Storage Classes and Lifecycle Policies
content: Amazon S3 stores objects in buckets and is designed for eleven nines of durability. Storage classes trade retrieval speed for price: S3 Standard for hot data, S3 Standard-IA for infrequently accessed data and S3 Glacier for archival. Lifecycle policies automatically transition objects between classes or expire them after a set number of days. Versioning protects against accidental overwrites.

title: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) in the Apache Log4j Library
content: CVE-2021-44228, known as Log4Shell, was disclosed in December 2021 and affected the Apache Log4j logging library used by a huge number of Java applications. An attacker could trigger remote code execution by getting a crafted JNDI lookup string written to a log. Mitigation required upgrading Log4j to version 2.17 or later and blocking outbound LDAP traffic.

title: What Are Containers?
content: Containers bundle an application together with the libraries it needs, using an image defined in a Dockerfile. An image is made of cached read-only layers, so small code changes rebuild quickly. Because every container uses the kernel of the host, containers start faster and use fewer resources than virtual machines with their own guest operating system.

title: Baking a Sourdough Loaf
content: Feed your starter the night before so it is bubbly and active. Mix flour and water, rest for an hour, then add the starter and salt. Stretch and fold the dough every thirty minutes, shape it, and let it proof overnight in the fridge. Bake in a preheated Dutch oven with the lid on for twenty minutes, then uncovered until the crust is deep brown.

title: Late Winner Settles the Derby
content: The home side looked tired in the second half, but a header from a corner in the ninetieth minute won the derby in front of a sold-out stadium. The visiting goalkeeper had made three outstanding saves earlier, and the manager praised the defence for holding a high line despite the wet pitch and the injury to the captain.

title: Growing Tomatoes on a Balcony
content: Tomatoes need at least six hours of direct sun, a deep pot and regular watering at the base rather than on the leaves. Pinch out side shoots on cordon varieties, tie the stem to a cane as it grows, and feed with a high-potassium fertiliser once the first flowers set. Water consistently to avoid split fruit and blossom end rot.
